young.html: Karl Barth (say BART) was a pastor in a small village in Switzerland. Every Sunday he had to preach, and every week he asked himself a hard question: what does the Bible really say?

Many teachers in his time read the Bible as a book about people searching for God. Barth, opening it again and again, came to believe it was the other way round: that the Bible is about God searching for people. He said reading it was like stepping through a door into a "strange new world."

young.cap: Two ways of reading, as Barth described them. Tap to switch the arrow.

young.html: Christians, Jews and others read the Bible in many ways, and families talk about it in their own way. This rung explains what Barth believed and why his ideas mattered so much in the 20th century.

A door into a book. Barth compared the Bible to a door into a house. Think of a book that felt like a door into another world for you. What did you find when you went through it? Draw the door and what lay behind it.

full.html: Karl Barth (1886–1968) was a Swiss Reformed pastor and theologian. He trained under the leading liberal theologians of Germany, who taught that Christianity was best understood through history, human religious experience and culture. In 1914, as the First World War began, many of those teachers signed a public statement supporting Germany's war policy. Barth was shaken: if theology could bend so easily to the mood of the age, something had gone wrong at its root.

As pastor of Safenwil (1911–21) he went back to the Bible, above all Paul's Letter to the Romans. His commentary on Romans (1919, rewritten in 1922) caused a sensation. The Word of God and the Word of Man collects addresses he gave from 1916 to 1923, published in German in 1924 and in English, translated by the American minister Douglas Horton, in 1928.

full.text: The strange new world within the Bible

We are to attempt to find an answer to the question, What is there within the Bible? What sort of house is it to which the Bible is the door? What sort of country is spread before our eyes when we throw the Bible open?
full.author: Karl Barth
full.work: The Word of God and the Word of Man, The Strange New World within the Bible (1916)

full.text: It is not the right human thoughts about God which form the content of the Bible, but the right divine thoughts about men.
full.author: Karl Barth
full.work: The Word of God and the Word of Man, The Strange New World within the Bible

full.name: gb-barth-direction
full.cap: The turn Barth made, in our own summary.

full.html: In a 1922 address to ministers Barth put the whole difficulty of his work in three sentences:

full.text: As ministers we ought to speak of God. We are human, however, and so cannot speak of God. We ought therefore to recognize both our obligation and our inability and by that very recognition give God the glory.
full.author: Karl Barth
full.work: The Word of God and the Word of Man, The Word of God and the Task of the Ministry (1922)

full.html: This style of thinking, which holds a "yes" and a "no" together, was called dialectical theology. Barth insisted God is "wholly other," not a higher version of human ideals, and can be known only as God speaks.

full.html: Barth became one of the most influential Protestant theologians of the century. In 1934 he was the main author of the Barmen Declaration, in which a group of German Protestants rejected the Nazi state's claim to control the church; he was soon forced out of his post at Bonn and returned to Switzerland. His Church Dogmatics, written from 1932 until his death and left unfinished, runs to more than 9,000 pages. Critics came from several sides. The liberal historian Adolf von Harnack, his former teacher, worried that Barth cut faith off from reason, history and culture. His ally Emil Brunner argued, against Barth, that people can know something of God through nature and conscience. Others, including Roman Catholic thinkers, admired his seriousness while disagreeing on key points. Readers of other faiths and of none have studied him as a major voice in 20th-century thought.
Thinking Barth simply rejected learning. He was a deeply learned scholar; his objection was to letting culture, rather than the Bible, set the terms of theology.

items: Augustine and Calvin, earlier on this ladder, are the theologians Barth read most closely; like them he put God's grace first.
Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling stressed the gulf between God and human reason; Barth drew on him in his early work and later moved away.
Schleiermacher and the liberal tradition grounded religion in human feeling; Barth's whole program answered them.
Pascal contrasted the God of the philosophers with the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; compare Barth's God who speaks.
When is it right for a religious group to say no to its own government?
Can people find out about God by reasoning, or only if God makes himself known?
Should faith change with the culture of its time, or stand apart from it?
How do we tell the difference between what we hope is true and what a text actually says?

questions: Barth was shocked when people he admired supported a war. Has someone you admired ever disappointed you? What did you do?
What is the difference between reading a book to find what you already think, and reading it to be surprised?
Barth said a preacher both must and cannot speak of God. Can something be a duty and also impossible to do perfectly?
In 1934 Barth helped write a statement refusing the government control of the church. Why might that have been dangerous?
How does your family talk about big questions of faith?
